sections.title: What is an Argument Turn?
sections.content: A turn is an advanced rebuttal technique where you take your opponent's argument and flip it to support your own side.
bullets: A turn is the strongest form of rebuttal
Link turns challenge the connection between the argument and the conclusion
Impact turns accept the argument but flip what it means

sections.title: Link Turns vs. Impact Turns
sections.content: A Link Turn argues that your opponent's evidence does not lead to their conclusion. An Impact Turn accepts their argument but argues the consequence is actually good for your side.
bullets: Link Turn: 'You say higher taxes reduce growth, but the data shows growth continued'
Impact Turn: 'You say higher taxes reduce profits. We agree — that is good, it pushes efficiency'
Link turns attack the connection; Impact turns flip the outcome

sections.title: Turning an Argument
sections.content: Motion: 'This house would ban plastic bags.'
sections.good:
Opposition: 'Banning bags hurts low-income families.'

Link Turn: 'Cities with bans provide free paper bags — the link to hurting families is broken.'

Impact Turn: 'Even if it creates inconvenience, that is a feature — it encourages sustainable habits that benefit everyone.'
sections.explanation: The Link Turn breaks the causal connection. The Impact Turn re-frames the outcome as positive.

sections.instruction: Opponent: 'Increasing minimum wage will cause fewer hires.' You respond: 'Studies show businesses raise prices or invest in productivity instead.' This is a:
options: Link Turn — breaking the causal connection
sections.feedback: This is a Link Turn — you challenge the assumption that higher wages lead to fewer jobs.

sections.q: What is the key difference between a Link Turn and an Impact Turn?
options: A Link Turn breaks the causal connection; an Impact Turn accepts it but flips the outcome
A Link Turn uses evidence; an Impact Turn uses emotion
sections.explain: Link turns attack 'A therefore B.' Impact turns accept 'A leads to B' but argue B is actually good.

sections.sentence: A {0} Turn accepts your opponent's evidence but argues the consequence is actually positive.
sections.instruction: Fill in the type of turn.
sections.feedback: Impact turns flip the evaluation — 'that's actually good for our side.'

sections.scenario: Debate about universal basic income. Opposition: 'UBI will reduce the incentive to work.'
sections.question: Which response is an Impact Turn?
options: UBI does not reduce work incentive — studies show recipients found more jobs
Even if UBI reduces work hours, that is positive — it allows education and caregiving
sections.feedback: This accepts the premise but re-frames it as positive — an Impact Turn.

questions.q: Why are turns considered the strongest form of rebuttal?
options: They are the hardest to execute
They turn the opponent's own argument against them
questions.feedback: Using the opponent's own argument against them is devastating — it undermines their entire position.
